title: Language-Instructed Vision Embeddings for Controllable and Generalizable Perception
claim: Static encoders give one fixed, entangled prediction; instruction-conditioned embeddings let users steer which aspect of the input is represented.
layout: Photo plus 3 bar charts, left-to-right; red instruction text under ours
description: On the far left is a photo of a green apple with a handwritten paper note reading "iPod" stuck to it. Next to it is a horizontal bar chart titled "State-of-the-art vision-only encoder (SigLip v2)". It ranks labels (iPod, Apple, Table, Fence, Backyard, Stem, Grass) by softmax probability, with iPod about 57% and Apple about 43%, so the model confuses the text with the object. Two more bar charts sit under the heading "Ours". Each has the same labels and light-blue bars. The first has a red italic instruction, "What is the fruit in the image?", and Apple dominates at about 85%. The second has "What is the text in the image?", and iPod dominates at about 77%. A "Language Instructions" label sits beneath the two charts. The eye goes first to the photo and then to the contrast between the bar charts.
caption: LIVE (Language-Instructed Vision Embedding). We show SoTA foundation model struggle to distinguish between textual content and objects within an image. LIVE enables userguided attention to specified aspects (e.g., “fruit” v.s. “text”), boosting control and prediction accuracy.
abstract: Vision foundation models are typically trained as static feature extractors, placing the burden of task adaptation onto large downstream models. We propose an alternative paradigm: instead of solely feeding visual features into language models, we use language itself to dynamically guide the vision encoder. Our method, Language-Instructed Vision Embeddings (LIVE), leverages language as high-level guidance to produce task-centric embeddings at inference time, removing the need for task-specific retraining. This enables the encoder to focus on contextually relevant aspects of the input, yielding more controllable and generalizable representations. Empirically, LIVE reduces visual hallucinations (+34 points on MMVP), surpasses vision-language models with orders of magnitude more parameters on visual question answering, and generalizes to unseen instructions and tasks -- offering a direct path toward adaptive, instruction-driven visual intelligence.
